headline: Halfway Rock holds the mackerel; bass working the ledges on the last of the ebb
subhead: Steady groundfish and a patient bass bite reward anglers who read the tide right around Casco Bay's structure this week.
body_markdown:
I anchored up on the northeast corner of Halfway Rock Tuesday morning, about an hour before dead low, and watched something I've seen a hundred times but never tire of: terns working a bait ball so tight to the granite you'd think they were going to fly into it. Mackerel, thick as I've seen them this season, holding right on the rock's edge where the current compresses against the ledge. That's the tell. When the birds are stacked that low and that close to structure, the mackerel are pinned against something, and where mackerel get pinned, bass and groundfish aren't far behind.

This is exactly the kind of week I expected when I said conditions would hold steady and typical for mid-summer Maine — and they have. The Gulf of Maine's cooler water is doing us a favor right now. While the water south of Cape Cod is pushing into the mid-70s and shoving striped bass onto deeper wrecks and night patterns, Casco Bay is still comfortably in that 66 to 70 degree window bass actually prefer. That keeps our fish on a more conventional daytime structure program — not explosive, but dependable, which for late July is about all you can ask.

The mackerel jigging at Halfway Rock has been the most consistent thing going. Small diamond jigs, quarter-ounce to half-ounce, no bait needed, dropped right to the edge of the ledge in 20 to 40 feet on the last two hours of the ebb. I had a father-son team out of South Portland tell me they filled a cooler in forty minutes Wednesday afternoon doing exactly that. Where you find those mackerel balled up, work a bucktail or a soft plastic — I like a 3-inch white shad body on a half-ounce jighead — just under the school. Bass have been intercepting stragglers on the drop, particularly on the last hour of the ebb into the first of the flood, when the current slackens enough for fish to hold position and feed without burning energy.

Striped bass around Peaks Island and the back side of Cushing have been a patience game this week rather than a numbers game. I'm marking fish on the sounder over the mussel beds off the eastern side of Peaks in 15 to 25 feet, but getting them to commit has meant slowing way down — a 1/2-ounce bucktail dressed with a chartreuse curl-tail, dragged dead slow on the bottom through the last of the outgoing. Harpswell's been similar. The ledges off Bailey Island — particularly that stretch running south toward the Punkin Nubble — have given up schoolie-to-mid-30-inch fish to guys drifting live mackerel under a slip float on the early flood, right as the tide starts to push bait back up onto the flats.

Cape Small has quieted some compared to two weeks ago, but it's still worth a stop if you're running that far south anyway. The rip that forms off the point on a moderate ebb has been holding fish, mostly in that mid-20s to low-30s range, taking topwater plugs at first light before the sun gets high enough to push them down.

Groundfish remain the backbone of the deeper water program, and that hasn't changed. Cod and haddock are still coming steady off the deeper structure around Halfway Rock — 80 to 110 feet on the northwest side where the bottom breaks hard — and off the ledges south of Bailey Island in similar depths. Jigging diamond jigs or bouncing a teaser-and-bait combo on the bottom during slack or the first hour of a tide change has been the most productive window; once the current really starts ripping through there, you spend more time re-rigging than fishing. Haddock have been running a bit smaller than I'd like this month, plenty of shorts mixed in, so bring a scale and know your minimums before you fill the cooler.

Bluefish remain scarce this far into the Gulf of Maine — the warm-water blitz pattern that's been tearing up the Jersey and Long Island beaches on peanut bunker simply hasn't pushed this far north, and with our water staying cool, I wouldn't expect it to. If you want bluefish, that's a trip south, not a Casco Bay trip.

Tide-wise, we're coming off the big pulls of the full moon and easing toward a neap cycle over the next several days, with the bay building back toward the August 12 new moon after that. That means somewhat gentler currents through the middle of next week — good news for anyone fishing bucktails on the bottom around Bailey Island or Cape Small, since the drift speed will be more manageable. It also means the mackerel schools may loosen up and spread rather than balling tight against structure, so if you're planning a Halfway Rock trip, I'd get there sooner rather than later in the week while the bait's still concentrated.

Looking ahead, I don't see any reason for this pattern to shift dramatically. Barring a passing thunderstorm — and early August around here usually throws at least one at us — expect the groundfish bite to stay steady on the deeper ledges, bass to keep working the shallower structure on the tide changes, and the mackerel to remain the reliable backbone of the week. If I had one morning to fish, I'd be back on that northeast corner of Halfway Rock an hour before low, watching for the birds.
